subject: mathematics
subtopic: Angle chasing: interior angles of regular polygons meeting at a point (tiling gap)
learning_objective: Compute the interior angle of a regular polygon and combine two of them with the fact that angles around a point sum to 360 degrees.
question: A tiling designer places one regular hexagonal tile and one regular octagonal tile flat on a table so that they share a complete common edge. At each end of that shared edge, three angles meet around the point: the interior angle of the hexagon, the interior angle of the octagon, and a gap that will be left uncovered. Find the size of this gap angle.
explanation: The interior angle of a regular n-gon is (n − 2)·180°/n. For the hexagon this is (6 − 2)·180°/6 = 120°, and for the octagon it is (8 − 2)·180°/8 = 135°. At the shared vertex, three angles fill the full turn around the point, so they sum to 360°. The uncovered gap is therefore 360° − 120° − 135° = 105°. (Equivalently, the gap equals the sum of the two exterior angles, 60° + 45° = 105°.)

option_analysis.A: Wrong: reports only the hexagon's interior angle (120°), again mistaking a single polygon angle for the gap.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: assumes the leftover space is a right angle (90°), a rough guess that ignores the exact interior-angle values and the 360° condition.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: adds the two interior angles (120° + 135° = 255°). This ignores that the three angles meeting at the vertex fill the 360° around the point, so the gap is the remainder, not the sum.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: reports only the octagon's interior angle (135°), treating one polygon's angle as if it were the gap.
option_analysis.E: Correct: hexagon interior = 120°, octagon interior = 135°; angles round a point sum to 360°, so the gap = 360° − 120° − 135° = 105°.

subject: mathematics
subtopic: Circle theorems: central angle = twice inscribed angle combined with the isosceles radii triangle
learning_objective: Apply the angle-at-the-centre theorem to obtain a central angle, then use the isosceles triangle formed by two radii to find a base angle.
question: A, B and C are three distinct points on a circle with centre O. The inscribed angle BAC, which stands on the chord BC, measures 34°. Find the size of the angle OBC.
explanation: The inscribed angle BAC and the central angle BOC stand on the same chord BC, so by the angle-at-the-centre theorem the central angle is twice the inscribed angle: angle BOC = 2 × 34° = 68°. Triangle OBC has OB = OC (both radii), so it is isosceles and its two base angles are equal. Hence angle OBC = (180° − 68°)/2 = 56°.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: gives the central angle BOC (68°) itself, stopping after doubling the inscribed angle and failing to carry out the isosceles-triangle step for angle OBC.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: computes 180° − 68° = 112° but forgets that the two base angles of the isosceles triangle are equal, i.e. omits dividing by 2.
option_analysis.C: Correct: central angle BOC = 2 × 34° = 68°; triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC), so angle OBC = (180° − 68°)/2 = 56°.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: uses the inscribed angle 34° directly as the apex of the isosceles triangle, (180° − 34°)/2 = 73°, forgetting to double the inscribed angle to obtain the true central angle.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: equates angle OBC to the inscribed angle BAC (34°), ignoring both the central-angle theorem and the isosceles triangle.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: mathematics
subtopic: Circle theorems: two tangents from an external point (tangent–radius) with the inscribed-angle theorem
learning_objective: Use the perpendicularity of a tangent and radius and the quadrilateral angle sum to find a central angle, then halve it with the inscribed-angle theorem for a point on the major arc.
question: From a point P outside a circle with centre O, two tangents are drawn, touching the circle at A and B. The angle APB between the two tangents is 48°. A further point C lies on the major arc AB. Find the size of the inscribed angle ACB.
explanation: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so angle OAP = angle OBP = 90°. In quadrilateral PAOB the angles sum to 360°, giving the central angle AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 48° = 132° (this is the angle subtending the minor arc AB). Point C is on the major arc, so the inscribed angle ACB stands on that same minor arc, and by the inscribed-angle theorem it is half the central angle: ACB = 132°/2 = 66°.

option_analysis.A: Correct: tangent–radius right angles give angle AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 48° = 132°; a point on the major arc gives ACB = 132°/2 = 66°.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: halves the tangent angle, 48°/2 = 24°, incorrectly treating angle APB as the central angle to be halved.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: reports the central angle AOB (132°) as the answer, omitting the halving step of the inscribed-angle theorem.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: uses the reflex central angle (360° − 132° = 228°) and halves it to 114°, effectively placing C on the wrong (minor) arc.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: sets the inscribed angle equal to the angle between the tangents (48°), confusing the tangent angle with the inscribed angle.

subject: mathematics
subtopic: Similar triangles: a line parallel to one side and the area ratio equal to the square of the side ratio
learning_objective: Recognise that a line parallel to a side creates a similar triangle whose area ratio to the whole equals the square of the corresponding side ratio, and invert this to find a length.
question: In triangle ABC, the point D lies on side AB and the point E lies on side AC, with DE parallel to BC. This divides the triangle into the smaller triangle ADE and the trapezium DBCE. The area of triangle ADE is 16 cm² and the area of the trapezium DBCE is 20 cm². Given that AD = 8 cm, find the length of AB.
explanation: Because DE is parallel to BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC. The area of the whole triangle ABC is 16 + 20 = 36 cm². For similar figures the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of corresponding sides, so (AD/AB)² = area(ADE)/area(ABC) = 16/36. Taking the square root, AD/AB = 4/6 = 2/3. Hence AB = AD × 3/2 = 8 × 3/2 = 12 cm.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: simply copies the given trapezium area (20) as the length, grabbing a number from the question without any similarity reasoning.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: uses the area ratio 16/36 as if it were the length ratio (AD/AB = 4/9), giving AB = 8 × 9/4 = 18 cm; this omits taking the square root of the area ratio.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: correctly finds the side ratio 2 : 3 but then multiplies AD by 3 (AB = 8 × 3 = 24), misreading the ratio AD : AB = 2 : 3 as a direct multiplier.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: compares triangle ADE to the trapezium (16/20 = 4/5) instead of to the whole triangle, giving AB = 8 × 5/4 = 10 cm.
option_analysis.E: Correct: area(ABC) = 36; (AD/AB)² = 16/36 so AD/AB = 2/3, giving AB = 8 × 3/2 = 12 cm.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: mathematics
subtopic: Intersecting chords length relation combined with the perpendicular-bisector property to identify a diameter
learning_objective: Apply the intersecting-chords length relation and recognise that a chord perpendicular to another chord at its midpoint passes through the centre, hence is a diameter.
question: Two chords AC and BD of a circle cross at right angles at a point P inside the circle. The point P is the midpoint of AC, with AP = PC = 6 cm, and BP = 4 cm. Find the radius of the circle.
explanation: By the intersecting-chords theorem, AP × PC = BP × PD, so 6 × 6 = 4 × PD, giving PD = 9 cm. Now P is the midpoint of chord AC, and chord BD is perpendicular to AC at P. The perpendicular drawn to a chord at its midpoint is the perpendicular bisector of that chord, and the centre of a circle always lies on the perpendicular bisector of any chord. Therefore the centre O lies on line BD, which means BD passes through the centre and is a diameter. Hence 2R = BD = BP + PD = 4 + 9 = 13 cm, so R = 6.5 cm.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: finds PD = 9 cm from the chord relation and stops there, reporting the segment PD as the radius.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: assumes AC is a diameter because P is its midpoint, giving R = AC/2 = 12/2 = 6 cm; being bisected by another chord does not make AC pass through the centre.
option_analysis.C: Correct: intersecting chords give PD = 36/4 = 9; since P is the midpoint of AC and BD ⟂ AC at P, line BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC and passes through the centre, so BD is a diameter, 2R = 4 + 9 = 13, R = 6.5 cm.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: mispairs the segments as AP × BP = PC × PD (6 × 4 = 6 × PD → PD = 4), then treats BD = 8 as the diameter to get R = 4 cm; the correct pairing multiplies the two parts of the SAME chord.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: correctly obtains the diameter BD = 13 cm but forgets to halve it to get the radius.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: mathematics
subtopic: Alternate segment theorem with a tangent parallel to a chord (arc-midpoint isosceles triangle)
learning_objective: Combine the alternate-segment theorem with the fact that a tangent parallel to a chord meets the circle at the midpoint of the arc (forming an isosceles triangle) to complete an angle chase.
question: The tangent to a circle at the point A is parallel to the chord BC of the same circle. A second chord AB is drawn, and the acute angle between the tangent and this chord AB is 58°. Find the size of the angle BAC of triangle ABC.
explanation: By the alternate-segment theorem, the angle between the tangent at A and the chord AB equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment, namely angle ACB; hence angle ACB = 58°. Because the tangent at A is parallel to the chord BC, the point A is the midpoint of arc BC, so the arcs AB and AC are equal and therefore AB = AC. Triangle ABC is thus isosceles with angle ABC = angle ACB = 58°. The remaining angle is angle BAC = 180° − 58° − 58° = 64°.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: doubles the tangent–chord angle (2 × 58° = 116°), or sums the two equal base angles and mislabels the total as the apex angle BAC.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: reports the alternate-segment (base) angle 58° directly as angle BAC, confusing a base angle of the isosceles triangle with its apex angle.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: takes angle BAC as the supplement of the tangent–chord angle (180° − 58° = 122°), an unjustified supplementary assumption.
option_analysis.D: Correct: alternate segment gives angle ACB = 58°; tangent parallel to BC makes triangle ABC isosceles (AB = AC), so angle ABC = 58° and angle BAC = 180° − 58° − 58° = 64°.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: computes 90° − 58° = 32°, wrongly invoking a tangent–radius right angle at A that does not apply to angle BAC.
